defs: King of the Greek gods and ruler of Mount Olympus, god of the sky, thunder, and law.
Youngest child of the Titans Cronus and Rhea; brother and husband of Hera.
example: Zeus hurled a thunderbolt at the giants who stormed Olympus.

defs: Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage and childbirth; wife and sister of Zeus.
Known for her jealous anger toward Zeus's lovers and their children.
example: Hera sent serpents to the cradle of the infant Heracles.

defs: God of the sea, earthquakes, and horses; brother of Zeus and Hades.
Wielder of the trident, who could stir storms or calm the waters at will.
example: Sailors poured wine into the waves to win Poseidon's favour.

defs: Goddess of agriculture, grain, and the harvest; mother of Persephone.
Her grief at Persephone's abduction was said to bring the barren winter.
Goddess of wisdom, strategic warfare, and crafts; patron of the city of Athens.
Born fully armed from the head of Zeus; companion of heroes such as Odysseus.
example: Athena guided Perseus on how to slay the Gorgon.

defs: God of the sun, music, poetry, prophecy, and healing; twin of Artemis.
Patron of the Oracle at Delphi, where his priestess delivered his prophecies.
Goddess of the hunt, wild animals, the moon, and chastity; twin of Apollo.
An eternal maiden who roamed the forests with her band of nymphs.
God of war, embodying its violence and bloodlust; son of Zeus and Hera.
Often scorned by the other gods for his recklessness in battle.
Goddess of love, beauty, and desire, said to have risen from sea foam.
Her favour and her wrath drove many mortals and gods into ruinous passions.
God of fire, blacksmiths, and craftsmanship; forger of the gods' weapons.
Cast from Olympus and left lame, he laboured at a forge beneath the volcanoes.
Messenger of the gods and guide of souls to the underworld; god of travellers, trade, and thieves.
Wearer of winged sandals, swift and cunning son of Zeus.
Goddess of the hearth, home, and family; the gentlest of the Olympians.
She kept the sacred fire of Olympus and yielded her throne to Dionysus.
God of wine, vegetation, ecstasy, and theatre; son of Zeus and the mortal Semele.
His frenzied followers, the Maenads, celebrated him in wild revels.
God of the dead and ruler of the underworld; brother of Zeus and Poseidon.
He abducted Persephone to be his queen in the realm of the dead.
Queen of the underworld and goddess of spring growth; daughter of Demeter and Zeus.
She spends part of each year below with Hades, marking the seasons.
Leader of the Titans who overthrew his father Uranus and ruled the cosmos.
He swallowed his children to forestall a prophecy, until Zeus deposed him.
Titaness and mother of the first Olympians; sister and wife of Cronus.
She hid the infant Zeus from Cronus, giving him a stone to swallow instead.
The primordial personification of the Earth and mother of all life.
From her came the sky, the sea, the mountains, and the Titans.
The primordial god of the sky; first ruler of the cosmos and father of the Titans.
He was overthrown and castrated by his son Cronus.
A Titan who shaped humankind from clay and stole fire from the gods to give to mortals.
For this defiance Zeus chained him to a rock to be tormented daily.
example: Prometheus suffered eternally so that humans might have fire.

defs: A Titan condemned by Zeus to hold up the sky for all eternity.
He briefly tricked Heracles into bearing his burden during the hero's labours.
The primordial void from which the first gods and the ordered cosmos emerged.
In myth it was the formless gap that existed before all things.
The primordial goddess of night, born from Chaos at the dawn of creation.
Even Zeus was said to fear offending her ancient power.
The primordial personification of darkness, born from Chaos.
His gloom filled the dark spaces of the underworld.
The deep abyss below the underworld, used as a prison for the Titans and the damned.
It was said to lie as far below Hades as the earth lies below the sky.
The greatest Greek hero, son of Zeus, famed for his superhuman strength.
He completed the Twelve Labours as penance and was later made a god.
example: Heracles strangled the Nemean Lion with his bare hands.

defs: A hero, son of Zeus, who beheaded the Gorgon Medusa.
He rescued Andromeda from a sea monster and turned his enemies to stone.
Legendary king and hero of Athens who slew the Minotaur in the Labyrinth.
He escaped the maze using a thread given to him by Ariadne.
The greatest Greek warrior of the Trojan War, nearly invulnerable in battle.
He was killed by an arrow to his one weak spot, his heel.
The cunning king of Ithaca whose ten-year voyage home is told in the Odyssey.
Famed for devising the Trojan Horse and outwitting many monsters.
Leader of the Argonauts who sailed in quest of the Golden Fleece.
With the sorceress Medea's help he overcame the trials set by King Aeetes.
A hero who tamed the winged horse Pegasus and slew the Chimera.
His pride led him to fly toward Olympus, and he fell back to earth.
A legendary musician whose song could charm beasts, trees, and stones.
He descended to the underworld to reclaim his wife Eurydice.
A Gorgon with snakes for hair whose gaze turned onlookers to stone.
She was slain by Perseus, who used a mirrored shield to avoid her eyes.
A monster with the head of a bull and the body of a man, kept in the Labyrinth.
It devoured tributes of Athenian youths until Theseus killed it.
A many-headed serpent that grew two new heads for each one cut off.
Heracles destroyed it by searing each stump as part of his labours.
The three-headed hound that guards the gates of the underworld.
Heracles captured it alive as the last of his Twelve Labours.
A fire-breathing monster part lion, part goat, and part serpent.
It was slain by Bellerophon riding the winged horse Pegasus.
A race of one-eyed giants; some forged thunderbolts for Zeus.
The most famous was Polyphemus, blinded by Odysseus.
A man-eating Cyclops, son of Poseidon, who trapped Odysseus in his cave.
Odysseus blinded his single eye and escaped beneath his sheep.
A monster with a lion's body, eagle's wings, and a woman's head, who posed a deadly riddle.
She destroyed travellers who failed to answer until Oedipus solved it.
A six-headed sea monster who seized sailors from passing ships.
She lurked across a narrow strait from the whirlpool Charybdis.
A monstrous whirlpool that swallowed and disgorged the sea three times a day.
Sailors steering past her risked the jaws of nearby Scylla.
A winged spirit with a woman's face and a bird's body that snatched food and people.
The Harpies tormented the blind seer Phineus until the Argonauts drove them off.
A creature whose enchanting song lured sailors to wreck upon the rocks.
Odysseus heard their song safely by binding himself to the mast.
A monstrous storm giant, the deadliest creature in Greek myth, who challenged Zeus.
Zeus defeated him with thunderbolts and buried him beneath a mountain.
A creature half beautiful woman and half serpent, called the mother of monsters.
With Typhon she bore the Hydra, Cerberus, the Chimera, and others.
A divine winged horse that sprang from the blood of the slain Medusa.
He was ridden by Bellerophon to defeat the Chimera.
A creature with the upper body of a man and the lower body of a horse.
Most were wild and savage, though the wise Chiron tutored many heroes.
A woodland spirit, part man and part goat, who followed Dionysus in revelry.
Satyrs were known for music, wine, and mischief.
A minor nature goddess inhabiting rivers, trees, mountains, or springs.
Nymphs often featured as companions of greater gods or lovers of heroes.
The highest mountain in Greece, believed to be the home of the twelve Olympian gods.
Its cloud-hidden peak held the palaces where the gods gathered.
The shadowy realm of the dead ruled by Hades, reached across the river Styx.
Souls were ferried there by Charon and judged for their lives above.
A blessed region of the underworld reserved for heroes and the virtuous dead.
There the souls of the righteous enjoyed eternal ease.
The fortified city besieged by the Greeks for ten years in the Trojan War.
It fell at last to the trick of the wooden Trojan Horse.
The sacred site of Apollo's most famous oracle, regarded as the centre of the world.
Pilgrims sought the cryptic prophecies of its priestess, the Pythia.
The river forming the boundary between the living world and the underworld.
The gods swore their most binding oaths upon its waters.
The food of the gods, said to confer immortality on those who ate it.
Together with nectar it sustained the deathless Olympians.
The drink of the gods, partner to ambrosia, granting immortality and vigour.
It was served to the Olympians at their feasts.
A priest or shrine through which a god revealed prophecy, most famously at Delphi.
Kings and heroes consulted the oracle before great undertakings.
The protective shield or breastplate of Zeus and Athena, bearing Medusa's head.
Its appearance struck terror into enemies on the battlefield.
The fleece of a winged golden ram, the prized object of Jason's quest.
It hung guarded by a sleepless dragon in the grove of Colchis.
A jar that, when opened by Pandora, released all the evils into the world.
Only hope remained inside once the lid was shut again.
A giant wooden horse in which Greek soldiers hid to enter and sack Troy.
Its name now stands for any deceptive ploy that hides a hidden threat.
The single vulnerable point of the warrior Achilles, his unprotected heel.
The phrase now means a person's one fatal weakness.
The goat-legged god of the wild, shepherds, and rustic music.
His sudden cries were said to inspire the sensation called panic.
The god of love and desire, whose arrows kindled passion in gods and mortals.
He is often shown as a winged youth with bow and quiver.
The goddess who personified victory in war and athletic contest.
She was depicted as a winged figure crowning the triumphant.
The goddess of the rainbow and a messenger of the gods, especially of Hera.
She travelled between heaven, earth, and the sea bearing divine words.
The goddess of magic, crossroads, the moon, and ghosts.
She was invoked in spells and worshipped at boundaries and doorways.
The Titan who personified the sun, driving his fiery chariot across the sky each day.
He saw all things and reported the abduction of Persephone to Demeter.
The Titaness who personified the moon, drawing it across the night sky.
She loved the sleeping shepherd Endymion.
The goddess of the dawn, who rose each morning to herald the sun.
She was called rosy-fingered for the colours of daybreak.
The god of medicine and healing, son of Apollo, trained by the centaur Chiron.
His skill grew so great that he could raise the dead, angering Zeus.
A wise and immortal centaur who tutored many Greek heroes.
Unlike his savage kin he taught medicine, music, and the arts of war.
The youth who flew on wings of wax and feathers made by his father Daedalus.
He flew too near the sun, the wax melted, and he plunged into the sea.
example: The fall of Icarus warns against reckless ambition.

defs: A master craftsman and inventor who built the Labyrinth of Crete.
He fashioned the wings that carried him and his son Icarus to freedom.
The first woman in Greek myth, fashioned by the gods and sent to mortals.
Her curiosity released the world's evils when she opened the forbidden jar.
The most beautiful woman in the world, whose abduction sparked the Trojan War.
Daughter of Zeus, she was queen of Sparta before fleeing with Paris.
A prince of Troy whose taking of Helen began the Trojan War.
He judged Aphrodite the fairest goddess in exchange for Helen's love.
The greatest warrior and prince of Troy, son of King Priam.
He was slain in single combat by Achilles outside the city walls.
The aged king of Troy during its siege by the Greeks.
He begged Achilles for the return of his son Hector's body.
The faithful wife of Odysseus who waited twenty years for his return.
She held off suitors by weaving and unravelling a burial shroud.
A sorceress who turned Odysseus's crew into swine on her island.
She later aided Odysseus after he resisted her magic.
A nymph who kept Odysseus on her island for years, offering him immortality.
She released him at last by command of the gods.
A Cretan princess who helped Theseus escape the Labyrinth with a thread.
She was later abandoned and became the bride of Dionysus.
A king granted the power to turn whatever he touched into gold.
The gift became a curse when even his food and daughter turned to metal.
A beautiful youth who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool.
Unable to leave it, he wasted away and became the flower that bears his name.
A nymph cursed to repeat only the last words spoken to her.
She pined away for love of Narcissus until only her voice remained.
The ferryman who carried the souls of the dead across the river Styx.
He demanded a coin as payment for the crossing.
The god of sleep, twin brother of Thanatos, son of Night.
He could lull even Zeus into slumber.
The personification of death, twin of Hypnos the god of sleep.
He carried the dying gently into the realm of Hades.
The goddess of strife and discord, sister and companion of war.
Her golden apple of discord set in motion the Trojan War.
The goddess who delivered retribution against arrogance and undeserved fortune.
She punished those whose pride offended the gods.
A Titaness, mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus.
Hounded by Hera, she found refuge on the island of Delos to give birth.
A Titaness of wisdom and cunning, the first wife of Zeus.
Zeus swallowed her, and their daughter Athena later sprang from his head.
The Titaness who personified memory and was mother of the nine Muses.
Poets invoked her so that the deeds of the past would not be forgotten.
A Titaness embodying divine law, order, and justice.
She was an early oracle and counsellor of the gods.
A Titan who personified the great river believed to encircle the world.
He and his wife Tethys fathered the rivers and the ocean nymphs.
A Titan of heavenly light, father of the sun, moon, and dawn.
His children were Helios, Selene, and Eos.
A Titan, father of Prometheus, Atlas, and other early figures.
He was regarded as an ancestor of humankind through his sons.
A Titan associated with the intellect and the axis of the heavens.
He was the father of Leto and grandfather of Apollo and Artemis.
One of the twelve Titans, sons of Uranus and Gaia.
He fathered several minor deities of the heavens and winds.
A Titaness of sight and the shining light of the clear sky.
She was the mother of the sun, moon, and dawn by Hyperion.
A Titaness linked with prophecy and the moon, grandmother of Apollo.
She was an early holder of the oracle at Delphi.
A Titaness of fresh water, wife of Oceanus.
She was mother of the rivers and the three thousand ocean nymphs.
Nine goddesses who inspired poetry, music, dance, and the arts and sciences.
Daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne, they were invoked at the start of epics.
Three goddesses who spun, measured, and cut the thread of each mortal life.
Even the gods were bound by the destinies they decreed.
Avenging spirits who pursued those guilty of grave crimes, especially against kin.
They hounded murderers and oath-breakers without mercy.
Goddesses of charm, beauty, and grace who attended Aphrodite.
They brought joy and refinement to gods and mortals alike.
A merman sea god, son of Poseidon, who heralded the waves with a conch shell.
His trumpet could raise or calm the storms of the sea.
A sea goddess and queen of the ocean, wife of Poseidon.
She personified the calm and the swell of the open sea.
A gentle, prophetic sea god known as the Old Man of the Sea.
Father of the Nereids, he could change his shape to escape capture.
A shape-shifting sea god who would foretell the future if held fast.
His name gives us the word protean, meaning ever-changing.
The god of the cold north wind and the bringer of winter.
He was depicted as a strong, winged, bearded figure.
The god of the gentle west wind and the herald of spring.
His mild breezes were thought to ripen flowers and fruit.
A king punished in the underworld with eternal hunger and thirst.
Food and water drew away whenever he reached for them, giving us the word tantalize.
A cunning king condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever, only for it to roll back.
His punishment stands for any endless, futile labour.
A king of Thebes who unknowingly fulfilled a prophecy to kill his father and marry his mother.
He answered the riddle of the Sphinx but met a tragic, ruinous fate.
A swift huntress who would only marry a man who could outrun her in a race.
She was beaten when a suitor dropped golden apples to slow her.
A princess chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea monster.
She was rescued by Perseus, who made her his wife.
A Trojan princess gifted with prophecy but cursed never to be believed.
She foresaw the fall of Troy, yet no one heeded her warnings.
The king who led the combined Greek armies against Troy.
He quarrelled with Achilles and was murdered on his return home.
King of Sparta and husband of Helen, whose loss launched the Trojan War.
He fought to reclaim her among the Greek host at Troy.
A towering Greek warrior at Troy, second only to Achilles in might.
He fell into ruinous madness after being denied Achilles' armour.
A powerful sorceress who helped Jason win the Golden Fleece.
Betrayed by him, she took terrible revenge upon his new bride.
The wife of Orpheus, who died from a serpent's bite.
Orpheus nearly led her back from the dead but lost her by looking back too soon.
A mortal princess, mother of Dionysus by Zeus.
She perished on beholding Zeus in his full divine glory.
A beautiful Trojan youth carried to Olympus to be cupbearer of the gods.
Zeus, taken by his beauty, granted him eternal youth.
Twin brothers, sons of Zeus and Leda, patrons of sailors and horsemen.
They were placed among the stars as the constellation Gemini.
A queen visited by Zeus in the form of a swan, mother of Helen.
Her children included the twins Castor and Pollux.
A princess carried off by Zeus in the shape of a white bull.
She bore Minos and gave her name to the continent of Europe.
A mortal woman loved by Zeus and turned into a heifer to hide her from Hera.
Hera set the hundred-eyed Argus to watch over her.
A giant with a hundred eyes set by Hera to guard the heifer Io.
After Hermes slew him, Hera set his eyes in the peacock's tail.
A blind prophet of Thebes renowned for his unerring foresight.
Even in the underworld he kept his power of prophecy.
A king of Crete who kept the Minotaur in the Labyrinth.
After death he became a judge of the dead in the underworld.
A youth who drove the sun chariot of his father Helios and lost control.
Zeus struck him down to keep him from scorching the earth.
A beautiful youth loved by Apollo and accidentally killed by a discus.
From his blood sprang the flower that bears his name.
A strikingly handsome youth loved by Aphrodite.
Killed by a wild boar, he became a symbol of beauty cut short.
The band of heroes who sailed with Jason aboard the ship Argo.
Together they braved many perils in quest of the Golden Fleece.
The vast maze built by Daedalus on Crete to hold the Minotaur.
Its winding passages were designed so that none could find the way out.
The horn of plenty, an endless source of food and abundance.
It came from a horn of the goat that nursed the infant Zeus.
The winged staff entwined with two serpents carried by Hermes.
It served as his herald's emblem and a symbol of his office.
A river of the underworld whose waters brought forgetfulness.
Souls drank from it to lose memory of their former lives.
A river of the underworld, often called the river of woe.
The dead were ferried across it on the way to Hades.
A meadow of the underworld where ordinary souls dwelt after death.
It lay between the torments of Tartarus and the bliss of Elysium.
The primordial god of the bright upper air breathed by the gods.
He personified the pure light of the heavens above the mortal sky.
A primordial god of the sea, born from Gaia at the dawn of creation.
He fathered many of the early sea deities and monsters.
The goddess of fortune and chance, who governed the prosperity of cities.
She could bestow good luck or sudden ruin without reason.
The goddess of youth and cupbearer of the gods before Ganymede.
She married Heracles after he was raised to Olympus.
A blind seer tormented by the Harpies, who fouled his food.
The Argonauts freed him in return for guidance on their voyage.
A handsome shepherd granted eternal sleep and unending youth.
The moon goddess Selene visited him as he slept.
A sea nymph loved by the Cyclops Polyphemus, though she loved the youth Acis.
When Polyphemus killed Acis in jealousy, she turned him into a river.
A skilled weaver who challenged Athena and was turned into a spider.
Her tale warns mortals against boasting they can rival the gods.
